title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
tagline: Tiny changes, remarkable results: the four laws of building good habits and breaking bad ones.

superpower.name: Habit Architect
superpower.description: You stack small daily wins into big results.

overview: Clear argues that results come from systems, not goals, and that habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. He breaks every habit into cue, craving, response and reward, and turns those into four laws: make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy and make it satisfying.

chapters.title: The Surprising Power of Atomic Habits
chapters.summary: Getting 1% better each day compounds into dramatic change over a year, while getting 1% worse quietly compounds into decline. Results often lag behind effort, so people quit in the 'valley of disappointment' before progress becomes visible. Clear argues that goals set direction but systems make progress: winners and losers often share the same goals, and what separates them is the daily process they follow.
keyIdeas: Progress is often invisible until it crosses a threshold.
chapters.tryThis: Pick one outcome you want and write down the daily process that would produce it.

quiz.question: According to Clear, what separates winners from losers who share the same goals?
quiz.explanation: Goals are shared; the daily system is what differs.

chapters.title: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity (and Vice Versa)
chapters.summary: Behaviour change works on three layers: outcomes, processes and identity. Most people start with outcomes; Clear says the deepest change starts with identity — deciding who you want to be. Every action is a vote for the type of person you become, and habits are how you cast those votes repeatedly until a new identity sticks.
keyIdeas: Build identity-based habits, not outcome-based ones.
Each action is a vote for who you are.
Decide the person you want to be, then prove it with small wins.
chapters.tryThis: Finish the sentence 'I am the type of person who…' and do one small thing today that proves it.

quiz.question: What is the deepest layer of behaviour change?
quiz.explanation: Lasting change starts with who you believe you are.

chapters.title: How to Build Better Habits in 4 Simple Steps
chapters.summary: Every habit runs through a loop: a cue triggers a craving, which drives a response, which earns a reward. The brain repeats loops that pay off. From this loop come the four laws of behaviour change: make it obvious (cue), make it attractive (craving), make it easy (response) and make it satisfying (reward). Inverting them breaks bad habits.
keyIdeas: Habits follow cue → craving → response → reward.
The four laws map onto the four steps.
Invert the laws to break a bad habit.
chapters.tryThis: Take one habit and label its cue, craving, response and reward.

quiz.question: Which law matches the 'response' step?
quiz.explanation: The response is the action itself; the easier it is, the more likely it happens.

chapters.title: The Man Who Didn't Look Right
chapters.summary: With enough practice the brain picks up cues automatically, which is why habits run without conscious thought. Before you can change a habit you must notice it. Clear suggests a Habits Scorecard: list your daily habits and mark each as helpful, harmful or neutral, and use 'pointing-and-calling' — saying actions out loud — to make the automatic visible.
keyIdeas: Use a Habits Scorecard to see your routines.
chapters.tryThis: Write down everything you do from waking until leaving home and mark each habit +, – or =.

quiz.question: What is the Habits Scorecard for?
quiz.explanation: It lists your habits so you can see which help or hurt.

chapters.title: The Best Way to Start a New Habit
chapters.summary: Vague intentions fail; specific plans succeed. An implementation intention states when and where you will act: 'I will [behaviour] at [time] in [location].' Habit stacking links a new habit to an existing one: 'After [current habit], I will [new habit].' Both give a new behaviour a clear, reliable cue.
keyIdeas: Plan the time and place for a new habit.
Stack new habits onto existing ones.
chapters.tryThis: Write one habit stack: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will…'

quiz.question: What is habit stacking?
options: Linking a new habit to an existing one
quiz.explanation: The current habit becomes the cue for the new one.

chapters.title: Motivation Is Overrated; Environment Often Matters More
chapters.summary: People choose things because of where they are, not only what they want. Small changes in what you see shape behaviour: put fruit on the counter, keep the guitar out of its case. Design your space so cues for good habits are visible, and give each space one main use so your brain links that place with that behaviour.
keyIdeas: Environment shapes behaviour more than willpower.
chapters.tryThis: Move one object so the cue for a good habit is the first thing you see.

quiz.question: What does Clear say matters more than motivation?
quiz.explanation: Designing your surroundings makes good behaviour the default.

chapters.title: The Secret to Self-Control
chapters.summary: People who seem disciplined are often just better at avoiding temptation. Once a habit is formed, its cue tends to trigger it regardless of willpower, so fighting it in the moment rarely works. The inversion of the first law is 'make it invisible': remove the cues of bad habits from your surroundings.
chapters.tryThis: Remove or hide the cue for one bad habit (move the phone charger out of the bedroom).

quiz.question: What is the inversion of 'make it obvious'?
quiz.explanation: Removing the cue stops the habit from starting.

chapters.title: How to Make a Habit Irresistible
chapters.summary: Dopamine rises in anticipation of a reward, so the expectation of pleasure drives us to act. The more attractive a habit is, the more likely it becomes. Temptation bundling pairs something you need to do with something you want to do, and can be combined with habit stacking.
keyIdeas: Pair a 'need to' with a 'want to'.
chapters.tryThis: Bundle a task you avoid with something you enjoy, like a podcast only while exercising.

quiz.question: What is temptation bundling?
options: Pairing a needed action with a wanted one
quiz.explanation: The enjoyable activity makes the needed one more attractive.

chapters.title: The Role of Family and Friends in Shaping Your Habits
chapters.summary: We imitate the habits of three groups: the close (family and friends), the many (the wider culture) and the powerful (people with status). One of the most effective ways to build better habits is to join a group where your desired behaviour is normal and you already share something with its members.
keyIdeas: We copy the close, the many and the powerful.
Join a group where your habit is the norm.
chapters.tryThis: Find one community where the habit you want is already ordinary.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three groups we imitate?
quiz.explanation: Clear names the close, the many and the powerful.

chapters.title: How to Find and Fix the Causes of Your Bad Habits
chapters.summary: Every behaviour has a surface craving and a deeper motive, like seeking connection, reducing stress or winning approval. Habits are modern ways of meeting those old needs. You can reframe a habit by highlighting its benefits ('I get to' instead of 'I have to'), and make bad habits unattractive by focusing on their costs.
keyIdeas: Make bad habits unattractive by seeing their costs.
chapters.tryThis: Rewrite one chore as 'I get to…' and notice how it feels.

quiz.question: How does Clear suggest reframing a hard habit?
options: Say 'I get to' instead of 'I have to'
quiz.explanation: Changing the mindset changes how attractive the habit feels.

chapters.title: Walk Slowly, but Never Backward
chapters.summary: Planning feels productive, but only action produces results. Habits form through repetition, not time, so the number of repetitions matters more than how long you've been trying. The goal is to practise, not to perfect: get your reps in.
chapters.tryThis: Stop planning one habit and do it, badly, five times this week.

quiz.question: What builds a habit according to this chapter?
quiz.explanation: Frequency of repetition, not elapsed time, makes a behaviour automatic.

chapters.title: The Law of Least Effort
chapters.summary: People naturally choose the option that takes the least work. Reduce the friction around good habits and add friction to bad ones. Prime your environment in advance — lay out workout clothes, prep ingredients — so the next action is effortless.
keyIdeas: We follow the path of least resistance.
Prepare the environment ahead of time.
chapters.tryThis: Set up tomorrow's good habit tonight so it takes one step to start.

quiz.question: What is the Law of Least Effort?
options: People choose the option needing the least work
quiz.explanation: So make good habits the easiest choice.

chapters.title: How to Stop Procrastinating by Using the Two-Minute Rule
chapters.summary: Many habits hinge on decisive moments that set the course of the next hours. The Two-Minute Rule says a new habit should take less than two minutes to start: 'read one page', 'put on running shoes'. Master showing up before optimising, because a habit must be established before it can be improved.
keyIdeas: Decisive moments steer the rest of the day.
Scale any habit down to two minutes.
chapters.tryThis: Shrink your target habit to a two-minute version and do it today.

quiz.question: What does the Two-Minute Rule say?
options: Start a new habit with a version under two minutes
quiz.explanation: Make starting so easy you can't say no.

chapters.title: How to Make Good Habits Inevitable and Bad Habits Impossible
chapters.summary: A commitment device is a choice made now that controls your actions later, like unplugging the TV or using a smaller plate. One-time actions — buying a good mattress, enrolling in automatic savings — lock in good behaviour, and technology can automate habits so they happen without effort.
keyIdeas: Make one-time choices that pay off for years.
chapters.tryThis: Make one one-time change today, like setting up an automatic transfer to savings.

quiz.question: What is a commitment device?
options: A choice now that controls future actions
quiz.explanation: It locks in good behaviour before temptation arrives.

chapters.title: The Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change
chapters.summary: What is rewarded is repeated; what is punished is avoided. Our brains favour immediate rewards, yet good habits often pay off later while bad habits pay off now. Add a small immediate reward to good habits — and make sure it doesn't contradict the habit's goal.
keyIdeas: Give good habits an instant pay-off.
chapters.tryThis: Attach a small, aligned reward to a habit you're building.

quiz.question: Why do bad habits stick easily?
quiz.explanation: Instant pleasure outweighs delayed costs in the brain.

chapters.title: How to Stick with Good Habits Every Day
chapters.summary: Habit tracking makes progress visible and satisfying: crossing off days builds a chain you don't want to break. When you slip, follow the rule 'never miss twice' — one missed day is an accident, two start a new habit. Be careful to track what matters, not just what's easy to measure.
keyIdeas: Track habits to make progress visible.
chapters.tryThis: Start a simple tracker and mark each day you do your habit.

quiz.question: What is the rule after missing a habit once?
quiz.explanation: One miss is fine; two in a row starts a new pattern.

chapters.title: How an Accountability Partner Can Change Everything
chapters.summary: To break a bad habit, make it immediately unsatisfying. A habit contract — a written commitment with a consequence, signed with an accountability partner — makes the cost of failure public and painful, which raises the stakes enough to keep you on track.
chapters.tryThis: Tell one person your habit goal and agree on a small consequence for missing it.

quiz.question: What is a habit contract?
options: A written commitment with a consequence
quiz.explanation: It adds a cost to breaking your promise.

chapters.title: The Truth About Talent (When Genes Matter and When They Don't)
chapters.summary: Genes don't decide your destiny, but they influence where you have an advantage. Choose habits and fields that suit your natural tendencies and personality. Exploration first, then exploitation: try widely, then focus where you find joy, progress and an edge — and create a niche by combining skills.
keyIdeas: Play a game that favours your strengths.
Combine skills to create your own niche.
chapters.tryThis: List three activities where you lose track of time — clues to your natural edge.

quiz.question: How should you choose where to compete?
options: Where your natural strengths give an edge
quiz.explanation: Align habits with your nature for faster progress.

chapters.title: The Goldilocks Rule: How to Stay Motivated in Life and Work
chapters.summary: People stay most motivated working on tasks at the edge of their ability — not too easy, not too hard. The biggest threat to success is boredom, not failure. Professionals stick to the schedule even when they don't feel like it; amateurs let life get in the way.
keyIdeas: Show up even when it's dull.
chapters.tryThis: Adjust one habit so it's slightly harder than easy but not overwhelming.

quiz.question: What does Clear call the greatest threat to success?
quiz.explanation: Mastery requires falling in love with repetition.

chapters.title: The Downside of Creating Good Habits
chapters.summary: Once habits are automatic you stop paying attention to small errors, so performance can plateau. Combine habits with deliberate practice and reflection: review your habits regularly and stay willing to update your identity as you grow, holding it loosely enough to change.
chapters.tryThis: Schedule a monthly 15-minute review of what's working and what isn't.

quiz.question: What is the downside of habits?
quiz.explanation: Reflection keeps automatic habits improving.
